| [THEORY-023](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-023.md) v4 | Current evidence cannot settle whether an AI system is conscious: mimicry undercuts behavioural evidence and architectural indicators presuppose the disputed computational functionalism, so the dispute is over what counts as evidence as well as the answer | Birch (2025), [LIT-111](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-111.md): behavioural markers are "gamed", and architectural markers are "Janus-faced", giving a two-level deadlock. | [THEORY-031](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-031.md) | The likelihood-ratio detector is optimal under the payoff, Neyman–Pearson and posterior criteria, which differ only in its threshold, so performance is an ROC and the criterion a point on it; d′ is criterion-free only for equal-variance normal signal and noise | Peterson & Birdsall (1953), [LIT-364](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-364.md) — the threshold on ℓ = f_SN/f_N is optimal for expected value and at fixed false-alarm rate, and the two optimum families coincide (Part I Thms 1–7). The separation of sensitivity from bias is a property of the model, not of the data. | Active |
| [THEORY-043](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-043.md) v6 | A mind of mindless agents and a mind of minded agents are one functionalist move run in two directions, and what separates them is an anti-nesting principle or an architectural criterion, neither yet principled | Minsky's society of mind builds a mind downward, out of agents that are not minds. Schwitzgebel ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)) builds a candidate mind upward, out of agents that are. The readings agree that agency survives both directions: Block grants a homunculi-head beliefs, List grants organised groups agency and awareness, Levin finds nested goal-pursuing collectives (his "Selves") at every scale. The dispute narrows to phenomenal consciousness, and every published way to accept the downward move while refusing the upward one is either an anti-nesting principle (Putnam's stipulation, IIT's exclusion postulate, Kammerer's functional version), each introduced for or justified weakly by the verdict it gives, or an architectural criterion that would count against a loosely coupled society of mind as much as against a nation. Proposed: an account of where a dispute stands, from philosophical argument and no measurement. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md) v2 | In relational frame theory the self is verbal behaviour's content, its process and its context, and the self as context is a perspective learned from deictic relations that cannot itself be found as content | Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) define three selves: the conceptualized self, the content of verbal relations about oneself; the knowing self, their ongoing process; and the transcendent self, their context. Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) say the third arises from deictic frames (I–you, here–there, now–then) as "a sense of self as a locus or perspective", and is "a context for verbal knowing, not the content", so its limits "cannot be consciously known". The account maps the three onto the record's holdings: the content is the narrative self (Dennett, Gallagher, Strawson), and the context is what Hume could not find among his perceptions and what Metzinger calls a transparent perspective. It differs from the minimal self (Gallagher) on origin: RFT says the perspective is learned in language. The evidence for the learned origin is cited, not read, so Proposed. The clinical claim is [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-048](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-048.md) | In explaining psychiatric disorder, biological findings implement psychological functions rather than replacing them | Kendler (2008), [LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md): following Marr, a lower-level theory either replaces a higher-level construct (temperature by mean kinetic energy) or implements it, and in psychiatry biology "will implement but not replace psychology". The thesis is argued from neuroscience's successes in perception, learning and memory, not from a psychiatric case, so it is Proposed. It is a thesis about explanation, not about distinct mental causes: it survives Pernu's argument ([LIT-147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md)) that the neural evidence supports only mental causation by identity. Kendler 2005 ([LIT-552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-552.md)), which argued the mind–brain propositions this paper develops, is unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-050.md) | Psychological inflexibility, in which verbal relations give private events aversive functions and make experiential avoidance a general strategy, is a transdiagnostic process in psychopathology | Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) model psychopathology as inflexibility: cognitive fusion supports experiential avoidance, which narrows behaviour. Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) give the mechanism: once a word stands in derived relation to an event it can carry that event's aversive functions, so private events become worth avoiding. | [THEORY-055](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-055.md) | An appraisal of an event's pertinence to the agent's concerns elicits the emotion, as a state of action readiness, and emotions differ by their mode of action readiness | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md), Frijda's own late statement of the theory of The Emotions ([LIT-546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-546.md), unread). An automatic appraisal of how an event bears on one's concerns elicits a state of action readiness: a motive to change one's relation to the object, with control precedence. Emotions differ by mode (hostility for anger, avoidance for fear), and "in the absence of concern pertinence … no emotion". It is the record's only read statement of an appraisal theory, because Lazarus ([LIT-550](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-550.md)) is unread. Both the elicitation claim and the claim that emotions differ by mode are argued, and neither is tested. The second is partly definitional within the theory. Rivals [THEORY-057](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-057.md): both accounts let instances vary and group them by function, but the appraisal account puts the unity in the agent's readiness and the constructionist account puts it in the perceiver's concept. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-056](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-056.md) v2 | Emotion regulation is not a process separate from emotion generation: most of it is one motive state checking another, with no distinct regulating system above them | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md), deny "the exclusivity of emotion regulation processes". Appraising the consequences of an impulse raises a competing readiness, as when fear of retaliation holds back anger, so control is the interaction of motive states and not reason governing emotion. Barrett (2017), [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md), reaches the second half from the opposite side of the emotion debate: automaticity and control are "different brain modes … not two battling brain systems", and she offers as a hypothesis that reappraisal works by the same predictions that construct emotion. Two rival theories of what an emotion is agree on this. Gross (1998), [LIT-554](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-554.md), poses the question and keeps the distinction. Proposed: argued from examples and from architecture, untested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-057](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-057.md) | Emotion categories are populations of variable instances grouped by the perceiver's concepts, not natural kinds with a shared neural or appraisal mechanism | Barrett (2017), [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md): degeneracy, population thinking, and a table of findings in which no region, network, pattern or neuron is consistent for an emotion category. From these she concludes that categories such as fear are populations of variable instances, grouped by a goal and constructed by categorization with a concept. She rejects basic-emotion and causal appraisal theories as positing a "Lockean essence". This is the record's only read statement of the view. The record's philosophy holdings sharpen it. Pernu ([LIT-147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md)) shows that many-to-one realisation at a fine grain does not rule out one variable at a coarser grain, so degeneracy alone does not carry the conclusion, and Table 1 has to. Searle ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md)) shows that Barrett's comparison with money is to observer-relative function, not to institutions. Rivals the appraisal account, [THEORY-055](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-055.md). Proposed: one theoretical paper, no independent test, and the reply unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-061](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-061.md) | In evidence-accumulation tasks, goals and instructions act on a decision by setting the parameters of the accumulation (drift, starting point or baseline, and threshold), not by specifying the response, and this holds for when to act as well as for which | Bogacz et al. Ratcliff and McKoon ([LIT-576](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-576.md)) find that the manipulations behave that way: speed or accuracy instructions are fitted by boundary separation alone, stimulus proportions mainly by starting point, difficulty by drift alone. Schurger et al. ([LIT-605](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-605.md)) carry the picture to the decision of when to move: the task goal raises the baseline toward threshold and leaves the moment to fluctuation. | [THEORY-063](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-063.md) | The unity of experience is the integration of one global world-model into a single functional cluster, and it does not require a self-model | Metzinger's précis of Being No One (2005), [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md): the globality constraint makes every conscious content part of one world-model. On the functional level that is "highest-order binding" into a single causal role, and on the neural level the prediction of "one single area of maximal causal density", after Tononi and Edelman's dynamic core. "What you subjectively experience upon experiencing your world as coherent is the high internal correlation strength between a subset of physical events in your own brain." A unified world comes before a self: the minimal case is "Selfless Snapshot Consciousness", and fully depersonalized states are "non-subjective consciousness". The neural half is a cited hypothesis, the précis says little is known, and how the cluster becomes one subject's is left open. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-064](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-064.md) | What is experienced as a self is the content of a self-model the system cannot recognise as a model, and nothing beyond such models is a self | Metzinger's précis of Being No One (2005), [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md), with his encyclopedia article "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)): a phenomenal self is a transparent self-model, one whose representational character "is not accessible to subjective experience", so that the system experiences its content "simply as ourselves". Transparency is graded, and the perspective itself is modelled, as a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation. The précis adds no evidence; its case studies are in the book, unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-068](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-068.md) | In a two-alternative choice made by two competing leaky accumulators, the decision is optimal only when leak and mutual inhibition balance, so that the network integrates the difference of the evidence without loss; imbalance bounds accuracy at any fixed time and weights early or late evidence | Bogacz et al. ([LIT-569](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-569.md)) prove that the pure drift diffusion model is the continuum limit of the sequential probability ratio test, and so the optimal two-choice decider, and that the linearised Usher–McClelland network reduces to it exactly when leak equals inhibition (and, for free response, when both are also large). Usher and McClelland ([LIT-565](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-565.md)) derived the difference of the two units as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with net leak K = k − β: K ≠ 0 caps accuracy, leak-dominant weights late evidence and inhibition-dominant early. Active because the core is derivation, checkable on paper. What it does not say: that brains are balanced, that the result carries to more than two options or to non-stationary evidence, or that the primacy and recency seen in six participants are explained by it. | Active |
| [THEORY-070](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-070.md) | How much cognitive control to exert, and on what, is decided by a cost-benefit computation (the expected value of control) in a specification system distinct from the structures that implement the control | Shenhav, Botvinick & Cohen ([LIT-585](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-585.md)) unify dACC's many reported functions as one: deciding whether, where and how much control to allocate. A control signal has an identity (a task set, a threshold, an attention template) and an intensity; its expected value is its probability-weighted payoff, with future value discounted, minus an intrinsic cost rising with intensity. dACC monitors and specifies; lateral prefrontal and subcortical structures implement. The paper reviews evidence and fits nothing, so Proposed. It does not say what the cost is, how EVC is computed, or that it governs emotion regulation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-088](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-088.md) v2 | Slow large-scale activity in human cortex is organised as in a pattern-forming medium: its flow is set by interacting spiral defects centred on phase singularities, which sit on boundaries between functional regions, annihilate with spirals of opposite rotation and repel those of the same | Xu, Long, Feng & Gong (2023), [LIT-638](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-638.md): in Human Connectome Project fMRI band-passed to 0.01–0.1 Hz, the cortical phase field holds about 16–19 spirals at a time around phase singularities, concentrated on boundaries between functional regions; their centres drift superdiffusively, opposite spirals annihilate (51% fully, 46% partly) and like ones repel (2.6%), and their positions and senses decode task condition above a raw-amplitude decoder. One source, fMRI only, at a spatial scale chosen because it maximised that decoding; the routing of activity flow is read from phase gradients and a phase-oscillator model, never perturbed. The kinship with Belousov–Zhabotinsky spirals and pattern-formation defects is the record's analogy, not the paper's. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-089](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-089.md) | The content of a mental representation has two factors, a narrow conceptual role inside the head and a referential factor relating it to the world, and a long-arm role theory that gets Twin Earth truth conditions right reduces to the same two | Block (1986), [LIT-648](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-648.md), and Block (1987), [LIT-625](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-625.md). Meaning has a conceptual-role component "entirely 'in the head'", an expression's "total causal role, abstractly described" in inference and decision, which twins share and which explains their behaviour, and an external component relating representations to referents and truth conditions. Conceptual role fixes the nature of the referential factor, not reference. A one-factor theory with long-arm roles must, to get Twin Earth truth conditions right, import normal context, causal chains of borrowed reference and experts; chop off what lies outside the skin and the rest is the short-arm role, so the difference is "merely verbal". Social meaning is assigned to the referential factor or to a third, social factor, and is only sketched. Proposed: no identity conditions for roles, and narrow content is given room, not shown explanatory. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-091](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-091.md) | A deficit in which consciousness and a capacity are lost together does not show that the capacity is a function of phenomenal consciousness, since access is lost too and the capacity is one the machinery of access has | Block (1995), [LIT-643](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-643.md), §6. Marcel, Flanagan, van Gulick and Schacter argue from the thirsty blindsight patient who does not reach for the water, and Searle from Penfield's petit mal automatisms, that a function of phenomenal consciousness is to let information guide action. In blindsight access is missing too, and in petit mal nothing shows experience is missing at all. "The fallacy is: an obvious function of the machinery of access-consciousness is illicitly transferred to phenomenal consciousness." That experience causes access, so that the function is experience's after all, is "a bold hypothesis, not a fallacy", and the deficit cannot decide it. Proposed: single-source, and the distinction it rests on is argued from conceivable cases. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-092](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-092.md) v2 | Behavioural capacity does not fix intelligence: a system with the capacity to respond sensibly to every possible input can lack it, so whether behaviour is intelligent, or the mark of any mental property, depends partly on how it is produced | Block (1981), [LIT-642](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-642.md): the strongest behaviourist conception of intelligence, a capacity to give sensible responses to any sequence of inputs, "whatever they may be", is met by a machine that stores every sensible conversation of a test's length and looks up its next reply, yet "the machine has the intelligence of a toaster". So psychologism is true: two systems alike in all actual and counterfactual behaviour can differ in intelligence through the processing that mediates it. Block (1995), [LIT-630](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-630.md), n. 1: the same machine refutes the wider claim that there is no mental difference without a behavioural one. It is a claim about constitution, not evidence: performance stays evidence for competence. It names no required kind of processing, and its machine is a lookup table, not a trained network. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-094](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-094.md) | Neither report nor no-report paradigms isolate the neural basis of consciousness, because post-perceptual cognition that tracks the percept persists without report; only a design that removes differential post-perceptual cognition does | Block (2007), [LIT-646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-646.md), framed the methodological puzzle: the neural basis of experience can be found only by deciding whether it includes the machinery of access, and the evidence comes through report. The no-report paradigm was the answer. Block (2019), [LIT-637](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-637.md), argues it has "a fatal flaw": subjects not asked to report still think about what they see, and that thought is aligned with the percept (the "bored monkey" problem). Eliminating report isolates the basis of experience "only if it eliminates post-perceptual cognitive processing" correlated with the percept. Brascamp et al.'s inconspicuous rivalry, whose switches subjects detected at chance, is the one such design Block offers. The method is specific to rivalry so far, and Block says there may be no general solution. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-095](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-095.md) | Phenomenal character is not fixed by long-arm functional role or by externally individuated representational content: on Inverted Earth it stays the same while both invert, so only internal accounts, short-arm functional or physical, remain open | Block (1990), [LIT-634](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-634.md): on Inverted Earth colours and colour words are inverted, so a subject fitted with inverting lenses notices nothing. After long residence, or for a twin with a molecule-for-molecule identical brain raised there, the intentional content of the experience of the sky inverts and so does its long-arm functional role, while qualitative content stays the same; Q = F₁, Q = F₂ and F₁ ≠ F₂ breaks transitivity of identity. Block (2003), [LIT-635](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-635.md), turns the case on externalist representationism: for colour there is no shared appearance property left to explain the sameness, and long-term memory blocks the gradual-shift reply, so "mental paint" is what stays the same. Proposed: both rest on an externalist shift of content and on first-person sameness, and Block concedes that a short-arm functional theory of qualia would escape. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-096](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-096.md) | Perceptual consciousness is global availability: a content becomes conscious when the activity it drives into a core of long-range hub neurons, prefrontal among them, crosses a threshold and ignites it, so that the network amplifies, sustains and broadcasts that one content to the specialised processors; below threshold it leaves a decaying wave and is not experienced | Mashour, Roelfsema, Changeux & Dehaene (2020), [LIT-631](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-631.md), a review by the theory's proponents. Conscious access is "a non-linear network ignition" that amplifies and sustains a representation so that local processors can access it, in a distributed core of long-range layer II/III and V pyramidal neurons with prefrontal cortex a key hub but "not ... the exclusive territory". Ignition is exclusive: one content at a time. Evidence: seen and unseen trials diverge after about 200 ms across modalities; in van Vugt et al.'s monkeys, missed stimuli drove V1 and V4 but only reported ones, and false alarms, ignited sustained prefrontal firing, and the signal-detection threshold is the ignition threshold. The review adopts the premise that global availability "is what we subjectively experience as a conscious state", and calls experience without access untested; that premise, not the access data, is where it rivals overflow and the sensory account. Single source, second-hand evidence, and the P3 question conceded open. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-097](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-097.md) | Long-range coordination in the human forebrain is carried by brief ripples that co-occur at distant sites: during them neurons co-fire more whatever the distance between them, and at retrieval they carry stimulus-specific reinstatement of encoding co-firing | Verzhbinsky, Daume, Cheng, Rutishauser & Halgren (2026), [LIT-633](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-633.md): in 1,373 single units from five bilateral forebrain regions of 35 epilepsy patients doing a Sternberg task, ripples (70–100 Hz, about 70 ms) co-occur between bundles at a median 5% at every tract distance from 71 to 223 mm, and unit pairs co-fire a median 34% more during co-ripples than in no-ripple periods, beyond a rate-only null and with no loss over distance. The gain rises with load (13% in maintenance, 19% at retrieval), and encoding co-firing for a stimulus recurs at retrieval in 0.29% of cell-pair trials in co-ripples against 0.14% outside them. Correlational throughout: one task, two load levels, clinically placed electrodes, nothing perturbed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-098](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-098.md) v3 | The neural basis of perceptual consciousness does not include the prefrontal machinery of cognitive access: it is recurrent activity in sensory cortex | Block's "back of the head" position, from three papers. Block (2005), [LIT-629](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-629.md): a phenomenal NCC (for seen motion, recurrent MT/V5–V1 activity) and an access NCC (frontoparietal broadcasting), with winner-take-all access letting a recurrent sensory representation lose and stay unaccessed. Block (2007), [LIT-646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-646.md): the mesh argument. If workspace activation is not part of the basis of experience, strong losing sensory coalitions explain why experience overflows access; if it is, nothing does. Block (2019), [LIT-637](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-637.md): no-report designs do not settle the prefrontal question, because thought about the percept persists, and one design that removes it found no prefrontal difference by fMRI, which Block calls evidence against prefrontalism while granting that ECoG could still support it. Proposed: an inference to the best explanation, with every experiment second-hand and the decisive test not yet run. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-100](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-100.md) | A neural correlate of conscious report does not require laminar cortex: in crows it is carried by the nidopallium caudolaterale, a nuclear pallial region whose neurons follow the reported percept rather than the stimulus | Maldarelli & Güntürkün (2025), [LIT-650](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-650.md), reviewing Nieder et al. NCL is nuclear, not layered; the cortex-like layers and columns found in birds are confined to the sensory pallium. So a correlate of conscious report does not need laminar cortex. | [THEORY-102](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-102.md) | In human ventral temporal cortex the category and object identity of a clearly seen, unchanging image are carried for as long as it stays on by a stable population code while activity amplitude decays; prefrontal and parietal content is a transient event at onset | Vishne, Gerber, Knight & Deouell (2023), [LIT-644](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-644.md): in 430 visually responsive subdural electrodes from 10 patients viewing images for 300–1,500 ms with no report on analysed trials, high-frequency activity and single-electrode category selectivity fell about 80% from peak by 800–900 ms, while the pattern across ventral temporal electrodes kept near-ceiling, time-invariant category and exemplar information that ended a fixed delay after the image went off. Prefrontal and parietal information was confined to about 150–600 ms and ignored duration. | [THEORY-103](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-103.md) v2 | Perceptual consciousness overflows cognitive access: in partial-report tasks more items are experienced than the roughly four that working memory holds, though any one of them can be accessed when cued | Block (2007), [LIT-646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-646.md), and Block (2011), [LIT-640](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-640.md). Subjects shown 8–32 items say they see all or almost all of them, report about 4, and when cued after offset can report or compare most of any cued subset: capacity 6–7 of 8 up to 1.5 s (Landman et al.), and 7, 6 and 5 of 8 at 1, 2.5 and 4 s (fragile visual short-term memory), against a working memory that stays at about 4. Block reads the surplus as experienced. The rival "sparse" reading holds it in an unconscious store plus a conscious generic or fragmentary image, and Block argues there is no independent evidence for either posit. Proposed: every experiment is second-hand, and that the surplus is conscious is the contested step. Overflow means most items are unaccessed, not that any is inaccessible. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-124](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-124.md) | During a visual decision task, neurons within a single area of mouse cortex rarely form discrete functional types, yet the task conditions the area distinguishes are linearly separable in nearly every way | Posani et al. (2026), [LIT-708](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-708.md): in about 14,000 cortical units of the IBL Brainwide Map, the 8-variable selectivity profiles of 4,617 selective neurons beat a covariance-matched Gaussian null for clustering within a region only in VISp, AUDp and SSp-ul. Elsewhere the profiles form an elongated, unclustered cloud. After merging conditions a region cannot tell apart (leaving 5 to 16 of 16), ≥ 95% of random balanced dichotomies are decodable above a shuffle null in 15 of 16 regions, GU being 0.82. Types do appear when regions are pooled, aligned with anatomy. One task, overtrained mice, a lenient separability criterion. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-125](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-125.md) | A group can itself be in an emotional state that is not its members' states in aggregation, when its distributed routines integrate the capacities an emotion requires into one action-oriented representation; because emotions are functional kinds such a state need not be felt, and no actual case has yet been shown | Huebner (2010), [LIT-702](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-702.md): a genuinely collective emotion is a state of a group that "could not be exhaustively characterized in terms of intentional states of individuals in aggregation". Fear requires danger detection, redeployment of attention, system-wide preparatory change and their coordination into one state with indicative content and imperative force; a distributed system can integrate routines that way. Some individual emotions are non-conscious, so a group's need not be felt, and emotion kinds are functional ("like vodka"), so lacking homologous mechanisms does not exclude groups. The paper establishes a possibility, not an instance: its worked case, the USS Palau crew, turns out to be "collective detection of danger in the absence of a fear response", and the replacement, the 2008 McCain–Palin campaign, is offered as "intuitively plausible" pending anthropological data. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-137](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-137.md) | Attributions of mental states to institutions, such as the knowledge that the collective knowledge doctrine of corporate criminal law attributes to a corporation no member of which held it, work largely by shaping the institutions to which they are made rather than by describing states they already had: the attribution holds the institution to a norm, the institution builds structures to meet it, and it becomes more predictable from the intentional stance, whether or not institutions really have minds | Tollefsen (2025), [LIT-736](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-736.md). Both sides of the group-mind debate treat ascription as tracking pre-existing causes. On the regulative view of folk psychology it shapes its target. In United States v. Bank of New England a court held a bank to know what no employee knew, and banks then built systems to detect reportable deposits. Narratives regulate too. Proposed: the regulative view is assumed, and the effect on banks is asserted, not documented. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-155](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-155.md) v2 | Iterated learning by Bayesian agents who sample from the posterior converges, in an ergodic chain, to the shared prior | Griffiths & Kalish (2007), [LIT-769](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-769.md), read in [NOTE-599](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-599.md): a chain of learners who share a prior and each sample a hypothesis from their posterior is a Gibbs sampler, so the probability a learner holds a hypothesis converges to its prior probability, whatever the amount of data passed on; with MAP learners the outcome centres on the prior's mode but depends on data amount and noise, and can amplify weak biases. It is a theorem about an idealized chain. It does not say human chains reach the prior, and Kirby, Cornish & Smith's laboratory chains, [LIT-771](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-771.md), are consistent with it without testing it. Whether human chains do is [QUESTION-137](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-137.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-163](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-163.md) v2 | In Zaslavsky, Kemp, Regier and Tishby's analysis, the colour-naming systems of the World Color Survey languages and English lie near the information-bottleneck bound for compressing perceptual meanings into words, at a trade-off parameter just above 1 and nearer than hue-rotated variants of themselves, with the need distribution over meanings estimated from the naming data | Zaslavsky, Kemp, Regier & Tishby (2018), [LIT-810](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-810.md), read in [NOTE-631](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-631.md): treating a colour lexicon as an encoder from Gaussian perceptual meanings to words, the World Color Survey languages and English lie near the IB curve of [LIT-338](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-338.md) at β ≈ 1.03, beat hue-rotated variants of themselves, and their soft, partly inconsistent naming is what IB optima look like. It does not show that languages are driven to the bound by any process, and the need distribution that makes the fit best is estimated from the naming data themselves. | Active |
| [THEORY-166](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-166.md) v2 | In the 66 Pew surveys of 2001–2011 that varied the order of two back-to-back binary questions, question order changed the answers but not the probability of giving the same answer to both, the equality a Lüders projection model predicts for any projectors; a classical model with order events can meet the same equality, so the regularity does not by itself favour quantum over classical probability | Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin & Busemeyer (2014), [LIT-795](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-795.md), on the QQ equality derived in [LIT-834](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-834.md): across the 66 Pew surveys of 2001-2011 that varied the order of two questions, question order shifts the answers (p = 0.0004) but not the probability that the two answers agree (p = 0.4625). The Lüders projection model predicts this without parameters, by a one-line identity. A classical model with order events can be built to satisfy the equality, and [LIT-264](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-264.md) shows that data meeting it are noncontextual, so it is evidence for a constraint on order effects, not for nonclassical probability or contextuality. A preregistered test with a constrained classical rival is [QUESTION-210](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-210.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-172](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-172.md) v3 | In Frank and Goodman's one-shot reference games, listeners' mean bets matched a parameter-free listener inverting a speaker who chooses among true utterances by informativeness, with a separately measured salience prior, and not salience alone; and in Bergen, Goodman and Levy's signalling games with novel symbols, listeners read a signal as excluding what the available alternative would have conveyed | Frank & Goodman (2012), [LIT-821](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-821.md), read in [NOTE-634](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-634.md): a parameter-free Bayesian listener inverting a size-principle speaker, with a separately measured salience prior, matches mean listener bets over seven context types at r = .99 (.87 without the 0 and 100 predictions), while salience alone correlates at r = .19. Bergen, Goodman & Levy (2012), [LIT-809](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-809.md), read in [NOTE-613](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-613.md): with novel signals and no conventions, listeners read the signal as the object its alternative did not name, and lexical uncertainty derives Horn's mapping. Goodman & Frank (2016), [LIT-816](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-816.md), states the framework. Shown for artificial games with given alternatives, by fits of condition means with no rival fitted; a test against named rivals on trial-level data is [QUESTION-209](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-209.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-208](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-208.md) | Agency is multiply realisable without cognition or mental states, and AI is a new kind of it | Floridi (2025), [LIT-897](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-897.md), read in [NOTE-702](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-702.md), with the criteria taken from Floridi & Sanders (2004), [LIT-898](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-898.md). In the record's reading, agency comes in kinds. All of them share interactivity, and the richer ones add graded autonomy and adaptability. The kinds are told apart by origin, mechanism and where their goals come from, not by intelligence. AI is computational agency with data-driven learning, serving goals set by humans, with no intelligence or mental states. Proposed: the paper assumes that AI is an agent, does not argue for this thesis over its rival, asserts that AI lacks intelligence, and never states the level of abstraction its comparison uses. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-220](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-220.md) | A far-from-equilibrium system that contributes to its own maintenance has functions relative to itself, with no history or observer needed, and one that switches among self-maintaining processes has indications of success that can be false by its own lights | Bickhard (2000), [LIT-1029](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1029.md), read in [NOTE-729](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-729.md). Function is contribution to a far-from-equilibrium system's own persistence; the asymmetry between persisting and decaying gives function and dysfunction, always relative to the system served, so a parasite's gut serves the parasite and harms the host. A candle flame has functions in this sense. Representation arrives with recursive self-maintenance: a system that picks its next interaction by how it has differentiated its environment implicitly predicates that the interaction will succeed, and can find the predication false. Proposed: a conceptual account, with no model, whose account of having a function (and so of malfunction) is deferred to another paper. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-245](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-245.md) | In a preregistered multimodal test with clearly seen images, prefrontal cortex carried a seen image's category but not its identity, and its orientation at most weakly, while posterior cortex carried all three; no prefrontal site responded at stimulus offset | Cogitate Consortium, Ferrante et al. (2025), [LIT-973](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-973.md), read in [NOTE-812](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-812.md). In iEEG and fMRI, with Bayesian support for the nulls, and against a positive control, prefrontal cortex held category but no identity or orientation, and none of 655 prefrontal electrodes showed the onset-and-offset response GNWT predicted. It does not show these dimensions were unaccessed, or that prefrontal cortex lacks them in other signals: high gamma and BOLD only, no single units, and every image was seen. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-255](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-255.md) v2 | In Aerts's subspace model of Hampton's membership data, and in any lattice whose membership weight is order-preserving, whatever its negation, taking concept conjunction and disjunction as meet and join cannot produce overextension or underextension, so a model of the guppy-type deviations must take conjunction as some operation other than the meet or drop the monotone weight, while the Kolmogorov-type deviations can be had from the meet of a non-Boolean subspace lattice | Aerts (2009), [LIT-934](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-934.md), Theorem 9 and §§2.2–3.3, read in full in [NOTE-808](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-808.md). The impossibility is a proof, and it needs only that membership is monotone in the subspace. The fits that place the k-type deviations in a tilted subspace lattice and the ∆-type ones in an emergent sector are models with free parameters, not tests. Negation appears only as the orthocomplement used to derive the conjunction model from the disjunction model; no negated concept is measured. | Active |
| [THEORY-261](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-261.md) v2 | In sparse distributed memory, recall of uniform random data from exact cues is a signal-to-noise problem whose optimum activates about (2MT)^-1/3 of the hard locations, and capacity then grows in proportion to the number of hard locations, rising toward about a tenth of them at 0.999 bit fidelity, not with the word length | Kanerva (1992), [LIT-921](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-921.md), §§3.5–3.7, read in full in [NOTE-779](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-779.md), after Jaeckel (1989a). An approximate derivation for uniform random data and exact retrieval cues. It does not cover noisy cues, which lower capacity, or clustered data, which the uniform design handles badly, and it does not contain the critical-distance analysis that is sometimes attributed to it. | Active |
| [THEORY-272](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-272.md) v2 | In Hopfield's 1982 simulations at N = 30 and 100, a network of threshold units with symmetric Hebbian couplings acts as a content-addressable memory whose stored random patterns are attractors: recall degrades severely near 0.15N patterns, a pattern placed 10 bits from another at N = 100 often fuses with it, and at 25-fold overload no stored pattern stays stable | Hopfield (1982), [LIT-918](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-918.md), read in full in [NOTE-819](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-819.md). The energy descent is derived for symmetric couplings; everything quantitative, including the 0.15N figure, the basin width and the merging distance, is simulation at N = 30 and 100. It does not say that spurious states come only from overload: they appear at a low load too. Nor does it say anything about addressed memory. | Active |
| [THEORY-330](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-330.md) | After a forced phase in which each person experienced every memory load from three to nine items, the load that had given that person the best reward rate predicted their later choices better than one item fewer or one more, in a copying task where items are seen once and cannot be looked up again; a steeper reward for long lists raised chosen load, a higher price for errors did not, and about one person in five kept choosing a non-optimal load | Howes, Duggan, Kalidindi, Tseng and Lewis (2016), [LIT-1062](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1062.md), read in [NOTE-882](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-882.md). Participants copied names shown one at a time from a mock email to a calendar. Each person's best list length in their own data predicted 55% and 46% of their choices, against 8–17% for the neighbouring lengths (N = 40 and 20). An exponential points schedule raised chosen length (6.99 against 5.07); forfeiting the whole trial on one error did not (5.00 against 5.05). 13 of 60 persistently chose a non-optimal length. There is no look-up and no model: the prediction is each person's empirical argmax. Lieder and Griffiths' description of it as a memorize-or-look-up trade ([LIT-1071](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1071.md)) does not fit the task. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-334](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-334.md) v2 | In copying a pattern of coloured blocks that stays in view, seven subjects told to work quickly looked back at the model about 1.3 times per block, and their commonest cycle, which looks at the model both before picking up a block and before dropping it, was the slowest per block in the authors' observed tallies (about 3 s, against 1.5 s for a cycle that copies from memory); looks fell to 1.0 per block with model and copy 70° apart and to 0.7 with one-colour patterns that could be chunked, and in three subjects a colour change made during a saccade raised fixation time by about 129 ms after pickup against about 50 ms before; no statistics are reported | Ballard, Hayhoe, Pook and Rao (1997), [LIT-1075](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1075.md), read in [NOTE-883](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-883.md). Fixations are modelled as pointers that bind a program's variable to a place in the world, so that only the task-relevant feature is fetched, just before use. In block copying, look-model, pick-up, look-model, drop was the commonest cycle (about 43% of cycles), at about 3 s a block against 1.5 s from memory; 70° separation cut looks from 1.3 to 1.0 per block, and one-colour patterns to 0.7. A colour changed mid-saccade mostly went unnoticed and cost time only once colour was held. The "carrying cost" of working memory is inferred from choice, not measured, and what is left in the world is raw input, not a computed result. Promoted 2026-10-20 on the observations alone (ADR-047 v3). | Active |
| [THEORY-335](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-335.md) | Selective accessibility, the account that comparing a target with a plausible anchor makes anchor-consistent knowledge more accessible and that this knowledge carries anchoring, fits moderations of the effect by applicability, representativeness and plausibility, but its accessibility step has not been measured: the lexical-decision test of it found nothing in five preregistered experiments, with a task that also missed direct priming | Strack & Mussweiler (1997), [LIT-1064](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1064.md), read in [NOTE-877](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-877.md), proposed the account and showed, in three small studies, that with the anchor number fixed the effect depends on whether the knowledge used to compare applies to the later estimate, and that plausible anchors slow the comparison and speed the estimate. Accessibility is inferred, never measured. Harris et al. (2019), [LIT-1067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1067.md), read in [NOTE-876](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-876.md), repeated the lexical-decision test of the accessibility step (Mussweiler & Strack 2000a, not held) five times at N = 128: anchoring was large and recognition of anchor-consistent words never moved (BF01 ≈ 21), but the same tasks missed direct picture priming. So the direct evidence is removed, not reversed; the account is neither refuted nor shown. Mussweiler & Strack 1999 ([LIT-1078](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1078.md)) is Unavailable. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-336](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-336.md) | An ideal observer is optimal relative to the information it is given, so a constrained ideal is the optimal decoder of a degraded input, not a restricted decoder of the full one; comparing real observers with ideals taken at successive stages of the visual system places losses by stage, and in early-vision tasks human performance is reported to parallel the retinal-stage ideal across conditions while falling well below it | Geisler (2011), [LIT-1055](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1055.md), read in [NOTE-870](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-870.md). A review that defines the ideal observer as optimal "given the available information and any specified constraints", and writes it as an expected-utility argmax over the posterior given the stimulus S or a constrained representation Z = g(S;θ). Constraints are added one at a time (optics, receptor sampling and noise, ganglion-cell summation), and human performance that parallels the retinal-stage ideal while falling below it is read as loss in central factors. The empirical parts are the review's account of studies the record has not read. The review gives no formula for efficiency and no notion of an optimum over a restricted class of computations. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-337](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-337.md) | In the comparative-question paradigm, judging whether a quantity is higher or lower than a high or low anchor pulls the later estimate of it toward the anchor, with large effects in five preregistered experiments of 128 people each, lasting through dozens of intervening word-recognition trials | Harris et al. (2019), [LIT-1067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1067.md), read in [NOTE-876](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-876.md), and Strack & Mussweiler (1997), [LIT-1064](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1064.md), read in [NOTE-877](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-877.md). In five preregistered experiments (N = 128 each) on temperatures and car prices, estimates after a high anchor exceeded those after a low one every time (d ≈ 0.85–1.39), with 40 to 70 word-recognition trials between the comparison and the estimate. Strack and Mussweiler's three small studies show the same effect, and that it can shrink or reverse when the knowledge used to compare does not apply to the estimate. This is the effect, not its mechanism: why the estimate moves is [THEORY-335](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-335.md)'s question and is not settled. | Active |
| [THEORY-339](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-339.md) | People's answers to a probability query depend on their own answers to an earlier query whose result it can use: a person's sub-answer predicts their later answer only when asked first, and a bias induced in a first judgment carries into a second only when the two share part of a hypothesis space, so reuse carries the earlier error with it; that reuse saves computation rests on one small response-time study and one secondary-task result | Dasgupta, Schulz, Goodman and Gershman (2018), [LIT-1074](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1074.md), read in [NOTE-875](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-875.md); Gershman and Goodman (2014), [LIT-1056](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1056.md), read in [NOTE-886](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-886.md); Dasgupta and Gershman (2021), [LIT-1077](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1077.md), read in [NOTE-865](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-865.md). In five small online experiments, an earlier answer shapes a later one only when the later query can use it, and errors in the first carry into the second. The authors call this amortized inference, reuse of past computation bought at a cost in bias. The speed benefit is shown once (median log-RT facilitation, n ≈ 50 per order) and otherwise assumed; storage and retrieval are free in the models; the 2021 review adds stale cached values from the planning literature, second-hand. No paper prices when reuse pays or touches stores outside the head. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-343](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-343.md) | In laboratory choice tasks, people offload cognition more as a task's internal demand rises, but the choice follows their evaluation of the demand rather than its benefit: they offload where it gives no gain and more when less confident at equal ability, and offloading can lower memory for what was offloaded | Risko & Gilbert (2016), [LIT-1059](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1059.md), read in [NOTE-887](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-887.md). A review: in choice/no-choice studies of rotated displays, delayed intentions and short-term memory, spontaneous offloading rises with internal demand, but it also occurs where it gives no gain (writing items down about 40% of the time at a two-item load already at ceiling), rises with lower confidence after ability is controlled, and differs between displays of equal measured demand. Expecting to have a result stored externally went with poorer memory for it. The review reports no effect sizes, the cited studies were not read, and its metacognitive model is an unformalised box diagram; the drift toward external reliance is a prediction, not a finding. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-346](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-346.md) | When information stays in view at a known place, people consult it less and rely on memory more as the time to reach it rises, in a graded trend across added delays from 0 to 3.2 seconds, even where the memory is weak and the display perfect; in one copying task a model that prices memory and display access in time alone, with no preference for either source, fits how many items people encode per look | Gray, Sims, Fu and Schoelles (2006), [LIT-1073](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1073.md), read in [NOTE-868](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-868.md), and Gray and Fu (2004), [LIT-1058](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1058.md), read in [NOTE-864](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-864.md). Adding a click to reach on-screen show information cut how often it was checked, and checks of finished settings came from memory. Lockouts of 0 to 3,200 ms on a Blocks World pattern cut looks and raised blocks placed per look, with linear trends. An ideal performer model with ACT-R memory equations and Q-learning on time alone fits four measures. That the control system has no bias toward the world is argued, not tested against a rival model. Errors in the 2004 study differed only against a group that memorized under several other changes, and the 2006 model has no wrong retrievals, no precomputation, no reuse across trials and no staleness. | Active |
| [THEORY-351](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-351.md) | In a two-pilot airliner cockpit, setting the approach speeds as bugs on the airspeed indicators, prepared 25 to 30 minutes ahead in a low-workload phase from a card selected by the displayed gross weight, turns recall and scale reading at the moment of use into a judgement of spatial proximity, so the cockpit system remembers the speeds without either pilot's memory being improved; this is argued by task analysis of mandated procedure, not measured | Hutchins (1995), [LIT-1066](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1066.md), read in [NOTE-867](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-867.md). A stylized task analysis of one airline's MD-80 procedure, informed by observation but reporting no measurements. The speed-card booklet, filtered by the displayed gross weight, is the system's long-term memory; the values pass through speech to bugs on two airspeed indicators, and on approach the pilots judge the needle's nearness to a bug instead of recalling and reading speeds. The paper concludes that the memory is "not made primarily of pilot memory". It analyses only success, for an anticipated, mandated and invariant task with a few values needed in a fixed order, so it says nothing about search for one item among many under a deadline. Cognition in the Wild ([LIT-1060](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1060.md)) is Unavailable. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-355](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-355.md) | Agents arrange their surroundings so that perception and choice take the place of internal search, changing how much thinking a task needs without changing what can physically be done; the set-up is paid once and recovered over the later choice points the arrangement serves, so an arrangement whose scope is the whole task can repay a large set-up and a narrow one must repay within the next few actions, and the arrangement decays unless maintained; the savings are argued and piloted, not measured | Kirsh (1995), [LIT-1076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1076.md), read in [NOTE-871](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-871.md), and Kirsh (1996), [LIT-1057](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1057.md), read in [NOTE-872](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-872.md). From video of cooks, assemblers and baggers and from informal observation, Kirsh classifies arrangements that simplify choice, perception and internal computation, frames their savings in search-complexity terms, and ties set-up cost to the number of choice points an arrangement serves. The 1996 paper adds a verbal investment rule with an interest factor for risk, one risk being that the change is not still present later, and upkeep against scatter. Neither paper gives a cost model or a measured saving; the 1995 paper says the savings do not "in general" admit meaningful quantitative estimation, and the 1996 paper puts mental cost outside its formalism. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-358](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-358.md) | In visual search among up to about 36 well-spaced items, a target that alone carries one colour or one distinctive shape part is found in time almost independent of the number of items, while a target identified only by a combination of features its neighbours carry separately takes time that grows linearly with the number of items, about twice as fast when the target is absent, the pattern of a serial self-terminating scan, and practice did not remove it; that conjunctions rather than similarity cause it is the paper's reading, not its result | Treisman and Gelade (1980), [LIT-1082](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1082.md), read in [NOTE-897](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-897.md). With coloured letters on cards of 1 to 30 or 36 items, a blue letter or an S among brown Ts and green Xs was found at 3.8 and 2.5 ms per item, and a green T among the same distractors at 28.7 ms per item when present and 67.1 when absent, linear and in the ratio of a scan that stops at the first find; 13 sessions of practice did not change it. The paper reads the contrast as feature integration: conjunction structure, not similarity, makes search serial. That reading is contested by the similarity account of Duncan and Humphreys ([LIT-1081](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1081.md)), which the record could not obtain, and it does not follow that any item unique in one attribute pops out in a real pile. | Active |
| [THEORY-359](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-359.md) | Cognitive mechanisms can be derived as the one, among those a brain can execute, that best trades the expected utility of its result against the opportunity cost of the time and resources it uses; the review shows the derivation reproducing many heuristics and biases, not that people are optimal, and the objective is per episode | Lieder & Griffiths (2020; online 2019), [LIT-1071](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1071.md), read in [NOTE-873](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-873.md). Resource rationality picks the heuristic that maximizes expected utility of its result minus the expected opportunity cost of the time and resources it uses (Eq. 3), averaged over environments consistent with what is known (Eq. 4), and a five-step method derives process models from it. The support is a review of others' models recast in this frame, with numbers from those studies. The authors offer optimality as a methodological device, not a claim about people, and the method lets constraints be refitted to data. The objective is per episode, with no terms for storing, retrieving or reusing a result, or for its going stale. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-360](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-360.md) | Tetris players rotate pieces more often and earlier than planning a placement and then executing it requires, rotating within a few hundred milliseconds of a piece appearing and checking the column more the higher the drop; Kirsh and Maglio read these moves as physical action standing in for mental computation at the moment of use, a saving argued from timing, not measured | Kirsh and Maglio (1994), [LIT-1054](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1054.md), read in [NOTE-878](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-878.md), with Kirsh (1995), [LIT-1076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1076.md), read in [NOTE-871](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-871.md). In Tetris keystroke data, pieces are rotated more than plan-then-act would need, rotation starts by 400–600 ms, and a translate-to-wall check precedes longer drops. The authors define an epistemic action as one whose primary function is to cut the space, time or unreliability of the agent's own computation, and argue these moves are of that kind. The saving is argued from a three-player pilot comparing physical with mental rotation, not measured in performance. The trade is offloading at the moment of use, once, with nothing stored; the paper sets itself against caching. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-402](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-402.md) | Collective intelligence is resource-bounded computation with a larger but modular budget: a group has more sensing, state, processing and action than any member, and pays coordination and cooperation costs because those resources sit in autonomous members, so the same trade-off yields groups that do better than their members on some tasks, groups that run qualitatively different algorithms, and groups that do worse | Pilgrim et al. (2025), [LIT-046](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-046.md), read in [NOTE-055](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-055.md), with Dreyer et al. (2024), [LIT-075](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-075.md) ([NOTE-040](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-040.md)), as its clearest instance. The paper offers a four-dimensional resource inventory, a catalogue of constraints and a mapping to mechanisms, and calls the known forms of collective intelligence "aspects of a single unifying principle". [NOTE-055](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-055.md) judges it a vocabulary, not a derivation: the resources have no metric, so the framework cannot say in advance when costs outweigh gains, and its "predictions" are research questions. Filed Proposed as the account the vocabulary states. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-433](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-433.md) | Whether a machine thinks is best replaced by whether a digital computer can play the imitation game as well as a man, because the reasons for withholding thought from a machine that does would equally withhold it from other people, whose thinking we also infer from what they say; the objections from consciousness, mathematical limits and informality of behaviour fail on that test or rest on unproved premises | Turing (1950), [LIT-394](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-394.md), read in [NOTE-355](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-355.md). The imitation game is offered in place of a definition of thinking, not as a test of it, and Turing says he has "no very convincing arguments of a positive nature". The account's force is the other-minds parity of §6.4, which assumes, as §2 states and does not argue, that the machine's best strategy is to answer as a man would; a machine built to imitate human output is the case that assumption does not cover. It makes no claim about consciousness. Proposed, and a rival of Block's psychologism. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-436](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-436.md) | Pain is a functional state of a whole organism, possessing a certain functional organisation as a probabilistic automaton, rather than a brain state, and this is the more plausible empirical hypothesis because one pain predicate applies to physically different organisms; the hypothesis keeps swarms out only by a stipulated condition that no pain-feeler has parts that separately possess the organisation | Putnam (1967), [LIT-396](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-396.md), recorded as Skimmed in [NOTE-335](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-335.md) from a course excerpt of the 1975 reprint, which carries the four-clause hypothesis verbatim; the original is Unavailable here. Proposed, and resting on that excerpt and on a result discussed throughout the literature the record holds. Clause (1) is empty by Putnam's own admission, since everything is a probabilistic automaton under some description, and clause (3), the anti-nesting condition, is introduced with one motive, to rule out swarms of bees. The argument against the brain-state view is comparative plausibility, not evidence. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-438](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-438.md) | The understanding deep networks reach is characteristically fractured: it can be real, by the test of stable tracking under structure-preserving perturbation, but it is symbolically misaligned, non-reductive, locally fractured, proxy-dependent and representationally fragmented, because the loss rewards any predictive patchwork and does not press it to unify | Freeborn (2026), [LIT-131](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-131.md), read in [NOTE-123](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-123.md). The Fractured Understanding Hypothesis is argued from four small demonstrations and cited literature, with no test of how common the five features are. The abstract names three features and §7.5 five. The paper also applies its own criteria inconsistently: its Othello verdict uses post hoc probes that it excludes from the agent. The definition of understanding it rests on is an explication, not a finding. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-454](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-454.md) | Perception is constitutively iconic, nonconceptual and nonpropositional and cognition paradigmatically discursive, and percepts are put to cognitive use only inside a 'cognitive envelope', the global workspace read as conceptualisation, where working memory holds recoded, task-dependent abstractions rather than the percepts themselves | Block (2024), [LIT-649](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-649.md), read in [NOTE-498](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-498.md): the précis of his 2023 book, not the book. The main thesis is stated and its arguments are in the book, unread here. The working-memory half is the update: nine cited lines of evidence that working-memory representations differ from perceptual ones and are task-dependent abstractions (moderate). The rereading of the workspace as conceptualisation rather than consciousness is asserted, not argued against the consciousness reading. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-458](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-458.md) v2 | Within the minimal self, the sense that a movement or a thought is mine and the sense that I am its source are distinct and come apart, as in involuntary movement and thought insertion; on Frith's comparator model the sense of agency depends on a forward model that precedes action and ownership on sensory feedback, so failed forward monitoring would explain thought insertion and, by the same mechanism, why first-person reference ordinarily cannot misidentify its subject | Gallagher (2000), [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md), read in [NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md) from the preprint. A review with no new results: the dissociation and the comparator account are reported from Frith, Haggard and others, and the link to the immunity principle is Campbell's argument, adopted and left conditional. It is about the minimal self, not the narrative self, for which the review's own proposal is two paragraphs. It does not say which minimal self, embodied or reflective, the analysis concerns. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-460](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-460.md) | Every leading reason to deny consciousness to current large language models except biology names a missing feature, recurrent processing, a global workspace, unified agency, world and self models or senses and embodiment, that engineering could add, so the case against current models is much stronger than the case against their extended successors; the one possibly permanent objection, biology, is the one the argument sets aside | Chalmers (2023), [LIT-411](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-411.md), read in full in [NOTE-345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-345.md). A classification of objections as temporary or permanent, argued by naming simple systems that have each feature. The credences that follow, under 10% for current models and 25% or more for conscious extended models within a decade, are illustrative by the author's warning, multiply stipulated factors under a disclaimed independence assumption, and depend on "mainstream assumptions". Biology is set aside with a reference to earlier work. It adds no evidence about any model. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-461](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-461.md) | If a substantial class of mental states, interoceptive, affective, perceptual and bodily-agentive, depends on an animate body, then today's text-only chatbots lack them and their self-ascriptions of such states are systematically untrue, and users can engage them without false belief by make-believe, as a new kind of interactive, self-involving and blended fictional character | Roberts (2026), [LIT-207](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-207.md), read in [NOTE-157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-157.md). The anti-realist half is a valid conditional whose antecedent, moderate embodied cognition, is assumed at prima facie strength. It covers body-dependent states only; footnote 8 allows realism about the chatbot as a disembodied thinker, so belief and reasoning are untouched. The fictionalist half shows the attitude permissible and apt, not required, and offers no evidence that users hold it. It is not a general denial that chatbots have minds. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-462](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-462.md) | If commonsense knowledge includes defaults that later evidence displaces, a monotonic logic, in which an added axiom can never remove a theorem, cannot represent that displacement as it stands; Minsky's further claim, that no consistency-seeking logical system can carry commonsense knowledge, is asserted, not shown | Minsky (1974), the frames memo, [LIT-410](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-410.md), read in [NOTE-337](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-337.md). Its appendix argues that "logistic" systems fail for commonsense on five counts, of which monotonicity is a correct observation about classical logic. That no repair is possible is asserted ("I think such attempts will continue to fail"), and consistency being undesirable is argued by analogy. The reading says the memo is a source of hypotheses, not evidence; this account takes from it only the half that holds by definition and marks the rest as the memo's claim. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-471](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-471.md) | Psychological states are not the machine-table states of an organism's unique best description as a probabilistic automaton, because some are never occurrent, several hold at once, there are indefinitely many and they contain one another, none of which a machine-table state can be; this leaves open that they are computational states of such a system | Block & Fodor (1972), [LIT-641](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-641.md), read in [NOTE-491](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-491.md). Five independent arguments against the machine-state identity theory, each with a stated escape that keeps functionalism: dispositions with no occurrent state, simultaneous states, too-fine individuation, productivity and constituent structure. They refute the machine-table clause, not functionalism. The paper's remaining argument (its third), inverted or absent qualia, is the only one aimed at functionalism broadly, and it is explicitly prima facie. | Active |
| [THEORY-472](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-472.md) v2 | A speaker who chooses words to minimise the information lost about a single intended referent, with words' literal meanings uniform over their extensions, picks each true word with probability inversely proportional to a power of its extension, so the size principle follows from informative communication; in one betting experiment, learners who knew the referent bet on a novel word's meaning in line with the inversion of that speaker (r = .93 on condition means), and in one free-description study speakers' word use followed it only weakly (r = .19) | Frank, Goodman, Lai and Tenenbaum (2009), [LIT-824](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-824.md), read in full in [NOTE-627](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-627.md). The derivation (utility −D_KL from intended to literal meaning gives P(w) ∝ \|w\|^(−α) for a point referent) is a proof under its assumptions. Learners' bets track the parameter-free inversion at r = .93 on condition means (700 web participants); speakers' tag-word use in free descriptions correlates at r = .19, .51 without colour terms and .02 for them. In these displays the informative-speaker learner and a plain size-principle learner coincide by construction, so the fit does not show that learners reason about the speaker. | Active |
| [THEORY-475](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-475.md) | In simulations from the drift-diffusion model itself, with 12 subjects and 20 to 150 trials each, hierarchical Bayesian estimation recovers every DDM parameter with less error than per-subject maximum likelihood, χ²-quantile fitting or non-hierarchical Bayes, most of all at few trials; whether the gain survives misspecification, and how much of the power gain is the hierarchy's, is not shown | Wiecki, Sofer & Frank (2013), [LIT-563](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-563.md), read in [NOTE-466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-466.md). Experiment 1 gives the lowest trimmed recovery error for HB on every parameter, and HB beat ML on the same data sets in every condition. Experiments 2–3 report more power to detect drift differences and trial-wise covariate effects, but HB was judged by a posterior-interval test and the others by t-tests, and the clean comparison was omitted. All data were generated from DDMs, with sz = st = 0. It is the standard partial-pooling result shown for one model family, not a test of the DDM. | Active |
| [THEORY-489](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-489.md) | Chains of human function learners, each trained on the previous learner's responses, forget their starting function and in 28 of 32 families converge within a few generations to a positive linear function, the bias earlier studies report, whatever function trained the first learner; this is convergence to the learners' favoured function, not shown to be convergence to their prior | Kalish, Griffiths & Lewandowsky (2007), [LIT-820](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-820.md), read in [NOTE-616](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-616.md). 288 participants in 32 nine-generation chains, four starting conditions. 28 families converged to a positive linear function; 3 converged to the negative linear one and 1 had not converged. The bias was taken from earlier studies, not measured on these learners, and stationarity was not established. It supports the claim that human transmission chains settle on what learners favour in this task, not that they reach the Bayesian prior, and it cannot tell sampling learners from MAP learners. | Active |
| [THEORY-500](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-500.md) | Ventromedial prefrontal cortex stores links between kinds of situation and the body states they produced, and re-enacting those states when an option is imagined marks it good or bad, overtly as a feeling or covertly as a bias, pruning the options before reasoning weighs them; without the marks, choice under uncertainty fails despite intact knowledge and intellect | Damasio (1996), [LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md), read in [NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md), the somatic marker hypothesis stated by its author; Bechara, Damasio, Tranel and Damasio (1997), [LIT-383](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-383.md), read in [NOTE-331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-331.md), the experiment it is usually cited for. The robust result is a group difference: in the gambling task all 10 controls and none of 6 ventromedial patients developed anticipatory skin conductance responses. That controls chose well before they knew, and that the marker causes the choice, is not carried by the statistics. The mechanism is argued, not observed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-512](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-512.md) | The extended-mind thesis worth disputing is that external entities partly constitute a subject's mental states in virtue of the subject's sensorimotor interaction with them; so stated it can reach standing belief but not consciousness, if consciousness needs information directly available for global control, since perception makes availability indirect | Chalmers (2019), [LIT-415](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-415.md), read in [NOTE-356](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-356.md), and his foreword to Clark's book (2008), [LIT-421](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-421.md), read in [NOTE-369](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-369.md). The 1998 thesis is satisfied by wired-in "extended circuits" that its critics accept, so the controversial thesis is constitution through perception and action. The perception-action boundary is then the strongest objection, met by revisionism, not refuted. Consciousness does not extend this way, on an imported criterion (direct availability, "not mediated by other mental states") and on the absence of any working twin case. Both halves are proposals defended against a few cases; the criterion is the author's earlier correlate of consciousness, not an argument made here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-520](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-520.md) | When coordination between two autonomous agents and the continuation of their encounter shape each other, the interaction gains an autonomy of its own, a precarious self-sustaining organization that lasts only while both agents stay autonomous; coordinating movement then coordinates sense-making, so some social understanding, such as recognising a partner, is a property of the interaction's dynamics and not of either individual | De Jaegher and Di Paolo (2007), [LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md), read in [NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md). A conceptual account built on coordination dynamics, with illustrative evidence: the corridor, charades, mother–infant timing and the perceptual-crossing experiments of Auvray et al., reported, not new. [NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md) declined a THEORY because the source carries no claim beyond its definition. The claim with some support is the perceptual-crossing one; the autonomy of the interaction is a definition, and the implications are called "speculative at this stage" by the authors. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-528](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-528.md) | The cases offered for extended cognition are explained at least as well by embedded cognition, on which the organism leans heavily on external props, and memory research finds that external stores lack the interference, generation effect and power-law learning and forgetting of internal memory, so a kind spanning both does no explanatory work and conservatism favours the embedded account | Rupert (2004), [LIT-422](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-422.md), read in [NOTE-343](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-343.md). The past-endorsement dilemma is strong: without it, directory assistance makes Otto believe every listed number; with it, the organism's endorsement is the final authority. The memory comparisons are moderate: the internal side is cited research, the external side is thought experiment, and no experiment on an external store is run or cited. The step from "different fine-grained kinds" to "no useful coarse kind" is a challenge plus conservatism. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-529](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-529.md) | A state is shown to be a representation by adaptation for transmitting information efficiently, near the optimal trade-off of rate, distortion and coder complexity under a teleofunctionally fixed distortion measure, rather than by correlation or mutual information alone, which nearly any causal link supplies and which cannot increase along a processing chain | Martínez (2025), [LIT-149](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-149.md), read in [NOTE-165](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-165.md): a position paper with no new theorem or data. Its sharpest point is a standard result: by the data-processing inequality, mutual information about a car/no-car decision can only fall from retina to IT, so a mutual-information criterion would place the decision at the earliest stage; explicitness is better read as ease of decoding. The rest is a proposal supported by selected examples. Complexity has no operational measure, teleofunctions are needed to fix the distortion measure or every system is efficient for some loss, and misrepresentation and engineered systems are not addressed. | Proposed |
