| [THEORY-538](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-538.md) | A system believes and desires when its behaviour is reliably and voluminously predictable by treating it as a rational agent with the beliefs and desires it ought to have, and the success of that strategy is an objective fact though adopting it is free; the more richly a system is connected to its world, the fewer interpretations fit, so thermostat and person differ in degree | Dennett, "True Believers", [LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md), read in [NOTE-353](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-353.md) in the revised text of 1987/1997. The criterion is substrate-neutral and silent on experience. Its adverbs are not quantified, the lectern is excluded only by gain over a baseline the essay leaves informal, and the Martian argument is an intuition pump that assumes the intentional patterns are not captured physically. "Most beliefs are true" rests on a way of counting beliefs Dennett doubts exists. Proposed, and a rival of both Block's psychologism and Searle's causal-powers account. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-541](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-541.md) | A model of discovery or analogy that is given representations built with the answer in view has been given most of the answer, as BACON was with Kepler's data and SME with its solar system and atom, and representation-building cannot be postponed to a separate module, because which representation is right depends on the task and on the analogy being made | Chalmers, French & Hofstadter (1992), [LIT-414](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-414.md), read in [NOTE-359](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-359.md) from the preprint, with Burns's review of Fluid Concepts (1995), [LIT-457](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-457.md), read in [NOTE-375](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-375.md). The BACON critique is strong; the SME critique moderate, with no alternative encoding run; the two arguments against a representation module informal. Burns turns the charges on Copycat: its Slipnet holds the domain's relevant relations, and the symbol-grounding objection to SME applies to it equally. Nothing is measured in either text. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-542](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-542.md) | A word learner that infers speakers' referential intentions jointly with the lexicon, and lets words be uttered non-referentially, learns object names from child-directed video more precisely than co-occurrence and translation models, and mutual exclusivity, word-guided object individuation and intention-guided mapping follow from it without principles built in for them | Frank, Goodman & Tenenbaum (2009), [LIT-815](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-815.md), read in [NOTE-611](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-611.md). On about twenty minutes of video from two dyads, annotated by the authors, the intentional model's lexicon scores precision .67 and F .55 against .06–.15 and .10–.22 for five baselines. The behavioural fits are qualitative, the baselines also produce mutual exclusivity, and the Baldwin case supplies the intention rather than inferring it. The reading said no THEORY, because the findings are specific to a small corpus and the record held nothing they correct; this account is filed Proposed for that reason. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-545](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-545.md) | Aerts and Gabora's founding quantum model of concepts is a classical probability model written in a Hilbert space: every context it uses is a projector diagonal in one basis, so the contexts commute and generate a Boolean algebra, its entangled 'pet fish' state gives the same statistics as a classically correlated mixture for every context in the model, and its guppy weights are copied from single-concept ratings rather than predicted for the conjunction | Aerts & Gabora (2005), Parts II and I, [LIT-312](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-312.md) and [LIT-340](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-340.md), read in [NOTE-299](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-299.md) and [NOTE-294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-294.md). The structural facts are checks of the published model, not of the authors' prose: contexts are sums of basis projectors, counts are chosen to match rounded frequencies, and the authors call the result a "quantization" of a set-theoretical model. Part I's mark of non-classicality (eq. 19) is met by Boolean projection lattices too, and its lattice structure is supposed, not derived. The model as printed is also infeasible in two cells. It does not say that no quantum model of concepts does better. | Active |
| [THEORY-547](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-547.md) | A language model idealized as continuing any text with a plausible next word from the collection of all plausible texts follows narrative coherence and not truth, so its false statements are confabulations within the story the context sets up; whether trained and aligned chat models keep that nature is an open empirical question the idealization does not settle | Bottou & Schölkopf (2023), [LIT-178](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-178.md), read in [NOTE-102](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-102.md): an essay offering imagery, with no evidence beyond one Vicuna-13b transcript pair. For the "perfect language model" it defines, insensitivity to truth follows from the definition. That deployed chat models share it is assumed, and the essay's own §2 leaves open whether alignment can turn a fiction machine into a verification machine. It credits the machine with knowledge of what makes sense in the story, denies it truth-directedness and intention, and never uses the word "sycophancy". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-558](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-558.md) | Moral judgment is usually caused by quick affective intuitions, and moral reasoning is usually a post-hoc search for supporting reasons that changes judgments mainly by triggering intuitions in other people | Haidt (2001), [LIT-511](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-511.md), read in [NOTE-403](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-403.md): the social intuitionist model. Its case rests mostly on non-moral evidence about automaticity, motivated reasoning and confabulation, carried over by argument. Its direct moral evidence is that harmless taboo violations are condemned and that affect predicts the condemnation better than perceived harm. The author calls it "a plausible alternative", not "an established fact". The disgust manipulations that were its direct causal evidence were later disputed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-563](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-563.md) | Consciousness is a real pattern in the brain's content-bearing states, a description that trades predictive accuracy for compression, and so coarse that describing the brain through it is metaphor; on that reading there is no Cartesian theatre, whether a given content was conscious can lack an answer when two descriptions compress and predict equally, and first-person reports are fallible as literal descriptions of the brain but authoritative as an author's | Taylor (2024), [LIT-461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-461.md), read in full in [NOTE-379](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-379.md). An interpretation of Dennett offered as consistent, explicitly not as correct or as what Dennett meant. Its argument for indeterminacy in masking rests on Dennett's idealised description of the cases, which Taylor calls "somewhat simplistic". It does not say which real pattern consciousness is, or what makes a real pattern a conscious one rather than a belief pattern. Filed as the account the reading states, at the strength the reading gives it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-564](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-564.md) | A bounded generative model can learn its own structure with no machinery beyond inference and learning: spare hidden-state slots with flat likelihoods get filled when an observation fits none of the learned causes, and Bayesian model reduction on the learned prior over states can return unneeded slots, though in a toy concept-learning task it recovers the true number of causes only 45–80% of the time unless the likelihood is given | Smith, Schwartenbeck, Parr and Friston (2020), [LIT-615](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-615.md), read in [NOTE-485](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-485.md). Expansion works in the toy domain over eight runs per condition, and only for novel stimuli. Reduction is the weak half: over 100 runs, the true number of concepts won in 45–80% of runs for four to seven, never for two or three, and in every run when the likelihood was given. Table 1 is the record's only measurement of how often reduction picks the generating structure when the parent model was itself learned. One initialisation; eight concepts, six binary features. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-570](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-570.md) | An emotional state is a large-scale selection of mental resources, switched on and off by Selectors that Critics trigger on recognising a type of problem, and so of the same kind as an intellectual way to think; feelings are the mind's descriptions of these cascades, and the body is one more resource the brain uses, not the substance of emotion | Minsky (2006), The Emotion Machine, [LIT-432](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-432.md), read in [NOTE-348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-348.md) from the author's 2005 draft. A design argued from examples, thought experiments and the author's own AI programs, with no experiment; Minsky marks several parts as his untested conjecture. It disagrees directly with the body-state views of emotion and of feeling. On Elliot it proposes the reverse causal order to Damasio's, with no evidence offered. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-573](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-573.md) | Signals of processing quality from different senses, such as fluency, familiarity and coherence, pool into one content-nonspecific feeling, and that pooled feeling contributes to the unity of conscious experience across modalities, alongside the integration of specific features; in support, coherence in one modality shifts judgments of regularity, familiarity and possibility about unrelated targets in another | Winkielman, Ziembowicz & Nowak (2015), [LIT-190](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-190.md), read in full in [NOTE-146](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-146.md). An opinion piece whose main evidence is the authors' own three experiments (Ziembowicz et al. 2013), summarised without statistics and not read by the record. The authors state that direct evidence is still needed that the effects run through changed experience and that its integration is causal. No study cited measures unity of experience. The LIT is itself Proposed; this account carries its promotion condition. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-577](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-577.md) | Our judgments that consciousness poses a hard problem are behaviour, so explaining them is an easy problem that can be solved without mentioning consciousness; and a theory that names a mechanism as the basis of consciousness owes an account of how that mechanism produces those judgments, which IIT and biological theories struggle to give, since a functional duplicate with zero integrated information, or in silicon, would make the same reports | Chalmers (2018), [LIT-425](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-425.md), read in full in [NOTE-354](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-354.md). The meta-problem follows from the physical explicability of behaviour; the challenge is a constraint argued from it, "not a knockdown argument". It assumes that a zero-Φ simulation has the same intuitions on a functional reading, which an IIT theorist can deny. The paper's own favoured solution, opaque introspective models attributing primitive relations of acquaintance, is "closer to a fleshed-out explanandum" than an explanation, and the data the programme needs mostly do not exist. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-579](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-579.md) | If belief is individuated by functional role, an external store that is constantly consulted, directly available and automatically endorsed can carry a standing belief, so the material vehicles of some mental states extend beyond the skin; the step from coupling to parthood rests on that premise and a parity principle the authors state rather than argue | Clark & Chalmers (1998), [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md), read in [NOTE-180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-180.md), with Clark's reply to the critics (2005), [LIT-403](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-403.md), read in [NOTE-363](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-363.md). Otto's notebook plays for him the role Inga's memory plays for her, so on role-functionalism it carries his standing belief, and Twin Otto, a duplicate from the skin in, believes otherwise. The constitutive step is carried by role-functionalism, the parity sentence and explanatory simplicity, none of them defended; the four coupling features mark a clear case and are explicitly not necessary and sufficient. Proposed: the step from causal coupling to parthood is the open point. The thesis is about vehicles of standing beliefs, not about consciousness. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-582](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-582.md) | Causal coupling between a process and something outside it does not by itself make that thing part of the process, so an argument from coupling to extended cognition needs a further premise saying what makes a process cognitive | Adams & Aizawa (2001), [LIT-438](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-438.md), read in [NOTE-368](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-368.md), and their reply to Clark (2010, read from a draft), [LIT-455](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-455.md), read in [NOTE-380](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-380.md). A thermostat's bimetallic strip, the kidney's filtration and a nerve at a neuromuscular junction are each coupled to more than themselves, and their processes do not extend. The 2010 text names the inference the "coupling-constitution fallacy". The point is that coupling does not entail parthood. It is not shown that coupling never accompanies parthood, nor that the extended-mind authors relied on coupling alone. | Active |
| [THEORY-588](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-588.md) | Lemma-based models of language production build in a lexicalist assumption, and the failure is algorithmic as well as representational: as long as retrieval of stored word-sized units and building of syntactic structure are separate stages, richer stored units cannot handle polysynthetic words, idioms whose parts syntax separates, or suppletion conditioned by an unplanned object | Krauska and Lau (2023), [LIT-031](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-031.md), read in full in [NOTE-029](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-029.md). A Hypothesis and Theory article with no new data and no implementation. Its diagnosis of named models (Levelt, the Consensus Model, lexically sized increments, treelets) is strong as textual analysis; the case that they fail on Inuktitut, Vietnamese collocations and Hiaki suppletion is argued from a few examples each, and Eberhard et al. are conceded to handle Hiaki in part. The 8-stage replacement model and its aphasia predictions are a verbal sketch, and this account does not rest on them. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-591](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-591.md) | Cognition has two necessary marks, involving non-derived content and a distinctive kind of causal processing, and as a contingent fact only processes in the brain have both, so notebooks, screens and tools coupled to a thinker are not parts of cognition, and human-plus-tool systems will support no science of their own | Adams & Aizawa (2001), [LIT-438](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-438.md), read in [NOTE-368](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-368.md), restated against Clark in 2010, [LIT-455](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-455.md), read in [NOTE-380](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-380.md) from a draft. Both marks are assumed: the first on a claimed consensus, the second on how mature sciences individuate kinds. The authors grant the parity principle and that cognition could extend; the claim is that it does not. The "no science of tool use" half is offered as a bet. Rupert, the other critic, rejects the derived-content argument as question-begging. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-593](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-593.md) | Perceptual learning can install perceiver-specific frames that change which objects a perceiver individuates from the same input, so cognition can shape the perceptual system over time while leaving open whether any single percept is cognitively penetrated | Ivy & Mroczko-Wąsowicz (2025), [LIT-099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-099.md), read in [NOTE-150](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-150.md). A conceptual proposal: a frame is installed by learning, often top-down, and then runs as a perceiver-specific structural principle of objecthood, so the system-level and episode-level questions about cognitive penetration come apart. The support is others' results reread through the concept, and one eye-tracking study of the authors'. The paper does not say what "bottom-up" means once priors sit in early processing, calls a frame "a specific top-down prediction" in §3.iii, and shows different weightings, not different objects. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-596](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-596.md) | To ascribe beliefs and desires is to predict a system by assuming it is rational and its beliefs mostly true, so a wholly false belief system has no coherent intentional description and contradictory beliefs no stable one, and the believer, like the person built on that notion, is an idealisation that real creatures only approximate | Dennett (1971), [LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md), read in [NOTE-350](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-350.md), and his reply to Stich (1980), [LIT-456](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-456.md), read in [NOTE-371](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-371.md). Belief ascription presupposes optimal design relative to goals, so "a false belief system is a conceptual impossibility" and, following Quine, the evidence for ascribing p is the best evidence against ascribing a contradictory q. In 1980 Dennett concedes the price: the intentional system, and the person, is "an unrealizable idealization". Argued from the logic of ascription and from evolution by assertion; no data. It is a claim about what ascription requires, not about what is in heads. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-601](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-601.md) | Among US undergraduates in the HERI surveys, students with higher verbal ability and stronger self-reported intellectual dispositions select into philosophy, and after adjusting for their entering SAT or freshman scores philosophy majors still score higher than other majors on GRE Verbal (SMD 0.48) and LSAT (0.35) but not on GRE Quantitative, and report more Habits of Mind and Pluralistic Orientation; the adjusted advantage is an association, not a shown effect of studying philosophy | Prinzing & Vazquez (2025), [LIT-155](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-155.md), read in full in [NOTE-167](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-167.md). HERI/CIRP freshman–senior data on 649,511 students at 804 institutions, 4,843 philosophy majors. Selection is real (SAT Verbal OR 1.57, SAT Math none). Baseline-adjusted mixed models and an IPTW check agree on the verbal and logical-test advantage and on its absence for quantitative tests. All test scores are self-reported, the SAT is an imperfect baseline for the LSAT, and nothing rules out faster verbal growth or harder test preparation among those who choose philosophy, so the paper's causal title is not part of this account. | Active |
| [THEORY-603](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-603.md) | In the Iowa gambling task, every one of ten controls and none of six patients with bilateral ventromedial prefrontal damage developed anticipatory skin-conductance responses, and three patients who could state the right strategy still did not switch to the good decks; the controls' preference for the good decks became significant only once they reported a hunch, so the study does not show advantageous choice or deck-specific bodily signals before any awareness | Bechara, Damasio, Tranel & Damasio (1997), [LIT-383](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-383.md), read in [NOTE-331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-331.md). The robust results are the group difference in anticipatory SCRs (Fisher's exact, one-sided P < 0.001) and the insufficiency of stated knowledge in three patients. The abstract's "before they realized which strategy worked best" and "before they knew" outrun notes 8 and 9: the pre-hunch choice preference was not significant, and the pre-hunch SCR effect reported is group × period, with no bad-versus-good deck test. Nothing here shows that the SCR, or what it indexes, causes the choice. | Active |
| [THEORY-608](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-608.md) | On one physical piano-movers puzzle scaled to the solver, ant groups solve better as they grow, while human groups barred from speech and gesture solve worse than individuals and talking groups only about as well as one; large ant groups keep speed and heading through wall contact, and the human mechanisms offered are fitted or observed informally, not tested | Dreyer et al. (2024), [LIT-075](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-075.md), read in [NOTE-040](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-040.md). Large ant groups (n = 28) reach about 90–100% success by 400 corridor widths, small groups (n = 48) about 50%. Restricted human groups do 32% worse than individuals' median, talking groups 7% better. There are no inferential statistics. The ant persistence mechanism is supported by collision data and a model whose carrier numbers fall short of calibration; the human majority vote (greediness P = 0.2) is tuned by eye, and "follow a random leader" rests on unrecorded observation. One ant species, one puzzle, one human population. | Active |
| [THEORY-609](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-609.md) | When implementing an automaton requires reliable, counterfactual-supporting transitions for every formal state, Putnam's construction fails, but any system with a clock and a dial still implements every inputless finite-state automaton, and any system with the right input–output dependencies, an input memory and a dial implements every finite-state automaton with those dependencies, so finite-state automata cannot carry computational sufficiency; combinatorial-state automata are argued, not proved, to escape | Chalmers (1996), [LIT-404](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-404.md), read in [NOTE-342](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-342.md) from the author's HTML copy. The failure of Putnam's construction and the clock-and-dial and input-memory theorems are constructive proofs given the definitions, so FSA-functionalism "still almost reduces to behaviorism". That a combinatorial-state automaton can be implemented only by the right fine-grained causal structure is a sketch: the obvious blind construction grows by a factor of n per step, and that every construction does is asserted. Logically possible false implementations and the one-region-per-component condition are left open by the author. | Active |
| [THEORY-616](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-616.md) | If a system has beliefs and desires just when attributing them, with rationality, predicts its behaviour well enough against rival theories, then the bearer of a language model's attitudes is the instance created by one context, not the model, the case that instances have them is presumptive and rests on tractability, and the best current desire hypothesis is helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness plus intrinsic desires a prompt installs | Goldstein & Lederman (2025), [LIT-206](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-206.md), read in [NOTE-138](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-138.md) from the preprint. Conditional on objective interpretationism, which the authors do not defend. The instance thesis is moderately argued; the presumptive case for attitudes rests on a tractability comparison never operationalised or measured; HHH+0 is "provisional", and its discriminating test is a conjecture. All the empirical support is second-hand and qualitative. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-636](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-636.md) | In vignette studies of US online participants, judgements that an outcome happened because the agent wanted it move with judgements that it was done intentionally when luck is manipulated, and predict them better than know-how or probability-raising do; but they account for only about half of the luck effect, and in one morally neutral case the two come apart | Quillien (2026), [LIT-132](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-132.md), read in [NOTE-092](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-092.md). Three Prolific studies (N = 198, 673, 142; ratings 1–7). Causation is the strongest predictor of intentionality (standardized β .46, .56, .53, against know-how .33, .20, .27 and probability-raising .14, .16, .10), and a pre-registered Knowledge × Process interaction predicted by the causal account holds (F(1, 423) = 32). The evidence is correlational, the mediation exploratory and partial (64%, 45%, 49%), and in the neutral Kraemer vignette causation shows no effect where intentionality does. The "model" is verbal; robustness is never measured. | Active |
| [THEORY-638](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-638.md) | Instantiating a formal program is never by itself sufficient for understanding or intentionality, since a person can carry out a program for answering questions in Chinese by hand without understanding Chinese; whatever thinks does so in virtue of causal powers at least equivalent to the brain's, and the reply that the whole system understands is answered only by an asserted internalisation | Searle (1980), [LIT-400](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-400.md), read in [NOTE-349](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-349.md) (target article only). The room is a full implementation run by a person, and his first-person verdict is read as the system's. The decisive step against the systems reply ("the system is just a part of him") is asserted, not shown, and which causal powers matter is left empirical. The argument is about understanding and intentionality, not consciousness, and it grants that machines, including artifacts with the brain's causal powers, could think. Proposed; Dennett's intentional strategy is its rival. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-646](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-646.md) | Skepticism about inner mental representations does not motivate fictionalism about folk psychology, because realism about beliefs as internal, intentional, causal states does not require the representational theory of mind; and a fictionalist who lets pretence yield genuine assertions about the overall state that causes behaviour is committed to that state | Drayson (2025), [LIT-112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-112.md), read in [NOTE-117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-117.md), against Toon's Mind As Metaphor (2023). Toon's negative argument needs "committed to internal, intentional, causal attitudes ⇒ committed to RTM", which non-representational functionalism (Lewis, Putnam, Loar) makes false; and his metasemantic case against inner representation mistakes one motivation for RTM for part of it. His positive argument faces a dilemma: a merely behavioural overall state gives fictionalism no causal advantage, and a causal one is a reason to identify it with the belief. It argues against two motivations, assumes fictionalism coherent, and sketches the functionalist alternative by citation in one paragraph. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-662](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-662.md) | The feeling of fluency is an inference about the precision of one's own processing, triggered by a change in precision against expectation; because its cause is internal and not given to introspection, a felt discrepancy is attributed to the most salient external source, as familiarity, liking or a sense of error | Brouillet and Friston (2023), [LIT-957](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-957.md), read in [NOTE-785](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-785.md). A perspective essay with no model and no new data. It joins Whittlesea's discrepancy-attribution hypothesis to precision-weighting. The part with moderate support is the reviewed finding that fluency judgements follow discrepancy from expected fluency (the hension effect and its extensions), reported secondhand. The precision reading and the felt/unfelt levels are proposals. "Felt" here means attended and reportable, not phenomenal, and fluency is not offered as affect. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-688](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-688.md) | In an actor-critic learner that can choose temporally extended options as well as primitive actions, options that fit the task speed learning, while options with ill-placed subgoals slow it, and options that fit an earlier layout keep the agent from finding a newly opened shortcut, so hierarchy helps only with the right subroutines | Botvinick, Niv and Barto (2009), [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md), read in [NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md). Toy simulations in a rooms domain with pre-trained options. Doorway options sped learning; window options slowed it; with a shortcut opened, primitive-only agents found the shortest path on 75% of runs while doorway-option agents never used it (mean 11.79 against 9.73 steps). It is a result about the model. That people or brains work this way is the separate, proposed account [THEORY-484](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-484.md). | Active |
